Or it is a reason for the forbidden act, meaning: do not do loud speech, for it leads to worthlessness. Thus al-Zajjaj's statement looks to the second aspect, not the first.

The clause ﴿while you do not perceive﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). In it is a severe warning and a great threat.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is not meant that the words "while you do not perceive" imply that a person may disbelieve while not knowing it. Just as a disbeliever does not become a believer except by his choosing faith over disbelief, likewise a disbeliever does not become a disbeliever through what he does not know.

Then He, glorified is He, encouraged compliance with what He commanded, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾. The root of *ghaḍḍ* is reduction from anything, and from it comes the reduction of the voice.

﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾. Al-Farra' said: He sincerely purified their hearts for piety, as gold is tested by fire, so that its good is separated from its bad and its impurity falls away.

Muqatil, Mujahid and Qatada said the same.

Al-Akhfash said: He singled them out for piety. It has also been said: He purified them from every ugliness. And it has been said: He widened them and made them spacious, from *maḥantu al-adīm*, meaning when you stretch the hide.

Abu 'Amr said: everything you exert yourself in, you have *maḥantahu* (tested it).

The *lām* in ﴿for piety﴾ (*li-l-taqwā*) is connected to an omitted element, meaning: fit for piety, as when you say, "You are fit for such-and-such." Or it is the *lām* of causation functioning as an explanation of the cause, as when you say, "I came to you for the fulfilment of a duty," meaning: so that my coming would be the cause of the fulfilment of the duty.

﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾. That is: those, for them. So it is a second predicate of the demonstrative (*ism al-ishārah*). It is also possible that it is a new sentence explaining what Allah has prepared for them in the Hereafter.

﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers—most of them do not reason﴾. They are the rude people of the Banu Tamim, as its explanation will come. *Warā' al-ḥujurāt* means outside them and behind them. *Al-ḥujurāt* is the plural of *ḥujrah* (room), like *al-ghurufāt* the plural of *ghurfah* (upper room), and *al-ẓulumāt* the plural of *ẓulmah* (darkness). It has been said that *al-ḥujurāt* is the plural of *ḥujar*, and *ḥujar* is the plural of *ḥujrah*, so it is a plural of a plural. A *ḥujrah* is a piece of land enclosed by a wall that surrounds it, and it is of the pattern *faʿīlah* in the sense of *mafʿūlah*.

The majority read *al-ḥujurāt* with a ḍammah on the *jīm*. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and Shayba read it with a fatḥah, as a lightening. Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with a sukūn. These are dialectal variants. The *min* in *min warā'* indicates the starting point, and there is no reason to prevent taking it in this sense.

﴿Most of them do not reason﴾, because ignorance overpowers them and coarseness is abundant in their natures.

﴿And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾. That is: if they had waited for your emergence and had not hastened to call out, it would have been more righteous for them in their religion and their worldly affairs, because in that there is observance of good manners toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), protecting his noble status, and acting in accordance with the veneration and exaltation he deserves.

It has also been said: they came as intercessors concerning captives, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) freed half of them and ransomed half of them. Had they been patient, he would have freed all of them. Muqatil mentioned this meaning.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, abundant in forgiveness and mercy, and extreme in both. He does not hold such people to account for what they neglected of good manners.

﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you a report, verify it﴾. The majority read *fa-tabayyanū* from *tabayyun*, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *fa-tathabbatū* from *tathabbut*. What is meant by *tabayyun* is investigation and examination, and by *tathabbut* is deliberation, avoiding haste, and looking carefully into the matter that has occurred and the report that has arrived until it becomes clear and evident.

The commentators said: this verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, as its explanation will come, if Allah wills.

His saying ﴿lest you harm a people in ignorance﴾ is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*). That is: out of dislike that you harm, or lest you harm, or lest you harm because the error of one who has not verified the matter nor deliberated about it is the most common, and it is ignorance, because it did not proceed from knowledge. The meaning is: being involved in ignorance regarding their situation.

﴿And then you become, regarding what you have done﴾ to them by harming them through error, ﴿regretful﴾ over that, distressed by it and concerned with it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, admonished them, saying: ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah﴾. So do not say a false word, and do not rush when news reaches you without verification. The *anna* and what follows it fill the place of the two objects of *i'lamū* (know). The clause ﴿if he obeyed you in much of the matter, you would be in distress﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *fīkum* (among you), or it is a new sentence. The meaning: if he obeyed you in much of what you report to him of false news, and what you suggest to him of opinions that are not correct, you would fall into *'anat*, which is hardship, toil, sin and destruction. But he does not obey you in most of what you want before the clarity of its aspect becomes evident to him, and he does not hasten to act on what reaches him before considering it.

﴿But Allah has made faith beloved to you﴾, that is: He made it the most beloved of things to you, or made it loved by you, so that nothing proceeds from you except what agrees with it and requires righteous matters and abandoning haste in reports and not verifying them. It has been said: the intended meaning of "these" is those other than the first group, to clear them of the attributes of the first group. The apparent meaning is that it is a reminder to all of what faith requires and what the love that Allah placed in their hearts necessitates.

﴿And has made it beautiful in your hearts﴾, that is: made it good through His success, until they act according to what it requires in words and deeds.

﴿And has made disbelief, defiance and disobedience hateful to you﴾, that is: He made everything that is of the kind of defiance and of the kind of disobedience hateful in your sight.

The root of *fisq* is departure from obedience, and *iṣyān* is the category of what Allah is disobeyed by. It has been said: by this He meant specifically lying, but the first is preferable.

﴿Those are the rightly guided﴾, that is, those described by what they have been mentioned for. *Al-rushd* is steadfastness upon the path of truth with firmness, from *al-rashādah*, which is a rock.

﴿As a bounty from Allah and favour﴾, that is: for the sake of His bounty and grace. The meaning is that He made beloved to you what He made beloved, and made hateful to you what He made hateful, for the sake of His bounty and grace, or He made you rightly guided for that reason. It has been said: the accusative is by an estimated verb, meaning: you seek bounty and favour.

﴿And Allah is Knowing﴾ of everything known, ﴿Wise﴾ in everything He decrees among His servants and determines for them.

Al-Bukhari and others reported from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr who said: "A caravan of the Banu Tamim came to the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Bakr said, 'Appoint al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad,' and 'Umar said, 'Rather, appoint al-Aqra' ibn Habis.' Abu Bakr said, 'You only intended to oppose me.' 'Umar said, 'I did not intend to oppose you.' So they argued until their voices were raised, and Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ until the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿do not put [yourselves] forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ that he said: they were forbidden to speak before His speech.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from 'A'isha concerning the verse that she said: "Do not fast before your Prophet fasts."

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* reported from her that she said: "Some people would precede Ramadan with a fast, that is, a day or two days. So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh also reported from her that "some people would precede the month and fast before the Prophet (ﷺ), so Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, the verse."

Al-Bazzar, Ibn 'Adi, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who said: "This verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, I will not speak to you except as a brother speaks in private conversation (al-sirar).'" In its chain (isnad) is Husayn ibn 'Umar, who is weak (da'if). However, it is supported by what 'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim narrated, and al-Hakim graded it sound (sahih), through the route of Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When this was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾, Abu Bakr said: 'By He who revealed the Book to you, O Messenger of Allah (p-1391), I will not speak to you except as a brother speaks in private conversation until I meet Allah.'"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Anas, who said: "When this was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ up to His words ﴿while you do not perceive﴾, Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas had a loud voice. He said: 'I am the one who used to raise my voice over the voice of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). My deeds have been nullified, and I am among the people of the Fire.' He stayed in his house, grieving. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) missed him, so some of the people went to him and said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has missed you. What is wrong with you?' He said: 'I am the one who raises my voice above the voice of the Prophet and speaks loudly to him. My deeds have been nullified, and I am among the people of the Fire.' They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of this. He said: 'No, rather he is among the people of Paradise.' Then, on the day of Yamamah, he was killed."

There are hadiths with a similar meaning on this topic.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words ﴿Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾, "the verse," that he said: "It was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas." Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from Abu Hurayrah concerning His words: "﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Among them is Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas.'"

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: with a sound chain (sanad sahih), through the route of Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from al-Aqra' ibn Habis, that "he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, come out to us.' He did not respond to him. He said: 'O Muhammad, indeed my praise is an adornment and my blame is a disgrace.' He said: 'That is Allah.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who call you from behind the private chambers﴾."

Ibn Mani' said: "I do not know of any sound (musnad) narration from al-Aqra' other than this."

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good (hasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, "concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, those who call you from behind the private chambers﴾, he said: A man came and said: 'O Muhammad, indeed my praise is an adornment and my blame is a disgrace.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'That is Allah.'"

Ibn Rahawayh, Musaddad, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: with a good chain (isnad hasan), from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "A group of the Arabs gathered and said: 'Let us go to this man. If he is a prophet, then we are the happiest of people with him; and if he is a king, we will live under his wing.' I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of what they had said. They came to his chamber and began calling out: 'O Muhammad, O Muhammad!' Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who call you from behind the private chambers, most of them do not understand﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took my ear and began saying: 'Allah has certainly confirmed your statement, O Zayd. Allah has certainly confirmed your statement, O Zayd.'"

There are hadiths on this topic.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mandah and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: with a fine chain (isnad jayyid), from al-Harith ibn Dirar al-Khuza'i, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he invited me to Islam. I entered it and affirmed it, and he invited me to zakat, and I affirmed it. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I will return to my people and invite them to Islam and the payment of zakat. Whoever responds to me, I will gather his zakat, and you, O Messenger of Allah, should send a messenger to me at such-and-such an appointed time (al-iban), so that he may take what I have gathered of zakat.' When al-Harith had gathered the zakat from those who had responded to him, and the appointed time came that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had intended to send to him, the messenger was delayed and did not come. Al-Harith thought that some displeasure (sakhtah) from Allah and His Messenger had occurred concerning him. So he summoned the leaders of his people and said to them: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had set a time for me, when he would send his messenger to collect what I had of zakat. There is no breaking of promise from the Messenger of Allah, and I do not see the delay of his messenger except as a result of displeasure. So let us go and come to the Messenger of Allah.'

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah to al-Harith to collect what he had gathered of zakat. When al-Walid set out and reached part of the way, he became frightened and returned. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Al-Harith withheld zakat from me and intended to kill me.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dispatched a force (ba'th) to al-Harith. Al-Harith came with his companions, and when the force set out and departed from Madinah, al-Harith met them. They said: 'This is al-Harith?' When he approached them, he said to them: 'To whom have you been sent?' They said: 'To you.' He said: 'Why?' They said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah to you, and he claimed that you withheld zakat from him and intended to kill him.' He said: 'No, by He who sent Muhammad with the truth, I did not see him at all, and he did not come to me.' When al-Harith entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: 'Did you withhold zakat and intend to kill my messenger?' He said: 'No, by He who sent you with the truth, I did not see him, and he did not see me. I only came when the messenger of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was delayed for me, and I feared that there had been some displeasure from Allah and His Messenger.' Then this was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, if a dissolute person brings you news﴾ up to His words ﴿Wise﴾."

Ibn Kathir said: "This is among the finest of what has been narrated concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse."

Many narrations have been transmitted agreeing that it was the occasion of the revelation of the verse and that it is what is meant by it, even though the accounts differ.

Or it is the *lām* of causation functioning as an explanation of the cause, as when you say, "I came to you for the fulfilment of a duty," meaning: so that my coming would be the cause of the fulfilment of the duty.

﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾. That is: those, for them. So it is a second predicate of the demonstrative (*ism al-ishārah*). It is also possible that it is a new sentence explaining what Allah has prepared for them in the Hereafter.

﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers—most of them do not reason﴾. They are the rude people of the Banu Tamim, as its explanation will come. *Warā' al-ḥujurāt* means outside them and behind them. *Al-ḥujurāt* is the plural of *ḥujrah* (room), like *al-ghurufāt* the plural of *ghurfah* (upper room), and *al-ẓulumāt* the plural of *ẓulmah* (darkness). It has been said that *al-ḥujurāt* is the plural of *ḥujar*, and *ḥujar* is the plural of *ḥujrah*, so it is a plural of a plural. A *ḥujrah* is a piece of land enclosed by a wall that surrounds it, and it is of the pattern *faʿīlah* in the sense of *mafʿūlah*.

The majority read *al-ḥujurāt* with a ḍammah on the *jīm*. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and Shayba read it with a fatḥah, as a lightening. Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with a sukūn. These are dialectal variants. The *min* in *min warā'* indicates the starting point, and there is no reason to prevent taking it in this sense.

﴿Most of them do not reason﴾, because ignorance overpowers them and coarseness is abundant in their natures.

﴿And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾. That is: if they had waited for your emergence and had not hastened to call out, it would have been more righteous for them in their religion and their worldly affairs, because in that there is observance of good manners toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), protecting his noble status, and acting in accordance with the veneration and exaltation he deserves.

It has also been said: they came as intercessors concerning captives, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) freed half of them and ransomed half of them. Had they been patient, he would have freed all of them. Muqatil mentioned this meaning.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, abundant in forgiveness and mercy, and extreme in both. He does not hold such people to account for what they neglected of good manners.

﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you a report, verify it﴾. The majority read *fa-tabayyanū* from *tabayyun*, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *fa-tathabbatū* from *tathabbut*. What is meant by *tabayyun* is investigation and examination, and by *tathabbut* is deliberation, avoiding haste, and looking carefully into the matter that has occurred and the report that has arrived until it becomes clear and evident.

The commentators said: this verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, as its explanation will come, if Allah wills.

His saying ﴿lest you harm a people in ignorance﴾ is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*). That is: out of dislike that you harm, or lest you harm, or lest you harm because the error of one who has not verified the matter nor deliberated about it is the most common, and it is ignorance, because it did not proceed from knowledge. The meaning is: being involved in ignorance regarding their situation.

﴿And then you become, regarding what you have done﴾ to them by harming them through error, ﴿regretful﴾ over that, distressed by it and concerned with it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, admonished them, saying: ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah﴾. So do not say a false word, and do not rush when news reaches you without verification. The *anna* and what follows it fill the place of the two objects of *i'lamū* (know). The meaning: if he obeyed you in much of what you report to him of false news, and what you suggest to him of opinions that are not correct, you would fall into *'anat*, which is hardship, toil, sin and destruction. But he does not obey you in most of what you want before the clarity of its aspect becomes evident to him, and he does not hasten to act on what reaches him before considering it.

﴿But Allah has made faith beloved to you﴾, that is: He made it the most beloved of things to you, or made it loved by you, so that nothing proceeds from you except what agrees with it and requires righteous matters and abandoning haste in reports and not verifying them. It has been said: the intended meaning of "these" is those other than the first group, to clear them of the attributes of the first group. The apparent meaning is that it is a reminder to all of what faith requires and what the love that Allah placed in their hearts necessitates.

﴿And has made it beautiful in your hearts﴾, that is: made it good through His success, until they act according to what it requires in words and deeds.

﴿And has made disbelief, defiance and disobedience hateful to you﴾, that is: He made everything that is of the kind of defiance and of the kind of disobedience hateful in your sight.

The root of *fisq* is departure from obedience, and *iṣyān* is the category of what Allah is disobeyed by. It has been said: by this He meant specifically lying, but the first is preferable.

﴿Those are the rightly guided﴾, that is, those described by what they have been mentioned for. *Al-rushd* is steadfastness upon the path of truth with firmness, from *al-rashādah*, which is a rock.

﴿As a bounty from Allah and favour﴾, that is: for the sake of His bounty and grace. The meaning is that He made beloved to you what He made beloved, and made hateful to you what He made hateful, for the sake of His bounty and grace, or He made you rightly guided for that reason. It has been said: the accusative is by an estimated verb, meaning: you seek bounty and favour.

﴿And Allah is Knowing﴾ of everything known, ﴿Wise﴾ in everything He decrees among His servants and determines for them.

Al-Bukhari and others reported from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr who said: "A caravan of the Banu Tamim came to the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Bakr said, 'Appoint al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad,' and 'Umar said, 'Rather, appoint al-Aqra' ibn Habis.' Abu Bakr said, 'You only intended to oppose me.' 'Umar said, 'I did not intend to oppose you.' So they argued until their voices were raised, and Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ until the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿do not put [yourselves] forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ that he said: they were forbidden to speak before His speech.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from 'A'isha concerning the verse that she said: "Do not fast before your Prophet fasts."

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* reported from her that she said: "Some people would precede Ramadan with a fast, that is, a day or two days. So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh also reported from her that "some people would precede the month and fast before the Prophet (ﷺ), so Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, the verse."

Al-Bazzar, Ibn 'Adi, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who said: "This verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, I will not speak to you except as a brother speaks in private conversation (al-sirar).'" In its chain (isnad) is Husayn ibn 'Umar, who is weak (da'if). However, it is supported by what 'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim narrated, and al-Hakim graded it sound (sahih), through the route of Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When this was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾, Abu Bakr said: 'By He who revealed the Book to you, O Messenger of Allah (p-1391), I will not speak to you except as a brother speaks in private conversation until I meet Allah.'"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Anas, who said: "When this was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ up to His words ﴿while you do not perceive﴾, Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas had a loud voice. He said: 'I am the one who used to raise my voice over the voice of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). My deeds have been nullified, and I am among the people of the Fire.' He stayed in his house, grieving. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) missed him, so some of the people went to him and said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has missed you. What is wrong with you?' He said: 'I am the one who raises my voice above the voice of the Prophet and speaks loudly to him. My deeds have been nullified, and I am among the people of the Fire.' They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of this. He said: 'No, rather he is among the people of Paradise.' Then, on the day of Yamamah, he was killed."

There are hadiths with a similar meaning on this topic.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words ﴿Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾, "the verse," that he said: "It was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas." Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from Abu Hurayrah concerning His words: "﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Among them is Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas.'"

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: with a sound chain (sanad sahih), through the route of Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from al-Aqra' ibn Habis, that "he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, come out to us.' He did not respond to him. He said: 'O Muhammad, indeed my praise is an adornment and my blame is a disgrace.' He said: 'That is Allah.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who call you from behind the private chambers﴾."

Ibn Mani' said: "I do not know of any sound (musnad) narration from al-Aqra' other than this."

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good (hasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, "concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, those who call you from behind the private chambers﴾, he said: A man came and said: 'O Muhammad, indeed my praise is an adornment and my blame is a disgrace.' Ibn Rahawayh, Musaddad, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: with a good chain (isnad hasan), from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "A group of the Arabs gathered and said: 'Let us go to this man. If he is a prophet, then we are the happiest of people with him; and if he is a king, we will live under his wing.' I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of what they had said. They came to his chamber and began calling out: 'O Muhammad, O Muhammad!' Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who call you from behind the private chambers, most of them do not understand﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took my ear and began saying: 'Allah has certainly confirmed your statement, O Zayd. Allah has certainly confirmed your statement, O Zayd.'"

There are hadiths on this topic.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mandah and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: with a fine chain (isnad jayyid), from al-Harith ibn Dirar al-Khuza'i, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he invited me to Islam. I entered it and affirmed it, and he invited me to zakat, and I affirmed it. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I will return to my people and invite them to Islam and the payment of zakat. Whoever responds to me, I will gather his zakat, and you, O Messenger of Allah, should send a messenger to me at such-and-such an appointed time (al-iban), so that he may take what I have gathered of zakat.' When al-Harith had gathered the zakat from those who had responded to him, and the appointed time came that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had intended to send to him, the messenger was delayed and did not come. Al-Harith thought that some displeasure (sakhtah) from Allah and His Messenger had occurred concerning him. So he summoned the leaders of his people and said to them: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had set a time for me, when he would send his messenger to collect what I had of zakat. There is no breaking of promise from the Messenger of Allah, and I do not see the delay of his messenger except as a result of displeasure. So let us go and come to the Messenger of Allah.'

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah to al-Harith to collect what he had gathered of zakat. When al-Walid set out and reached part of the way, he became frightened and returned. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Al-Harith withheld zakat from me and intended to kill me.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dispatched a force (ba'th) to al-Harith. Al-Harith came with his companions, and when the force set out and departed from Madinah, al-Harith met them. They said: 'This is al-Harith?' When he approached them, he said to them: 'To whom have you been sent?' They said: 'To you.' He said: 'Why?' They said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah to you, and he claimed that you withheld zakat from him and intended to kill him.' He said: 'No, by He who sent Muhammad with the truth, I did not see him at all, and he did not come to me.' When al-Harith entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: 'Did you withhold zakat and intend to kill my messenger?' He said: 'No, by He who sent you with the truth, I did not see him, and he did not see me. I only came when the messenger of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was delayed for me, and I feared that there had been some displeasure from Allah and His Messenger.' Then this was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, if a dissolute person brings you news﴾ up to His words ﴿Wise﴾."

Ibn Kathir said: "This is among the finest of what has been narrated concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse."

Many narrations have been transmitted agreeing that it was the occasion of the revelation of the verse and that it is what is meant by it, even though the accounts differ.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 49, verses 1–8 (part 1 of 2)**

It is Madani (revealed at Medina). Al-Qurtubi said: by scholarly consensus (*ijma'*).

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr that it was revealed at Medina.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾. The majority of readers read *tuqaddimū* with a dammah on the *tā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl* with a kasrah. In it there are two possibilities. The first is that it is transitive, and its object has been omitted in order to generalize, or the object has been left out to focus on the verb itself, as in their saying: "He gives and withholds" (*huwa yu'ṭī wa-yamna'*).

The second is that it is intransitive, like *wajaha* and *tawajjaha*. This is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ya'qub, *taqaddamū* with a fatḥah on the *tā'*, the *qāf* and the *dāl*.

Al-Wahidi said: *qaddama* here has the meaning of *taqaddama*, and it is intransitive.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the Arabs say, "Do not go forward before the imam" and "before the father" (*lā taqaddam bayna yaday al-imām wa-bayna yaday al-āb*), meaning: do not act hastily in the matter without him, and do not forbid [anything] without him, because the meaning is: do not go forward before their command and their prohibition. "Before the imam" is an expression for the imam himself, not for what is in front of a person. The meaning of the verse is: do not cut off a matter apart from Allah and His Messenger, and do not hasten in it.

It has also been said that the intended sense of "before so-and-so" (*bayna yaday fulān*) is his presence, because whatever a person is present for is "before him." ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in all your affairs, and within this falls abandoning going forward before Allah and His Messenger, as a primary inclusion.

Then He gave the reason for the command to taqwā (God-consciousness) in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ of everything heard, ﴿Knowing﴾ of everything known.

﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾. It is possible that the intended meaning is the literal raising of the voice, because that indicates a lack of modesty and an abandonment of respect, since lowering the voice and not raising it is among the requirements of veneration and honour.

It is also possible that the intended meaning is a prohibition of excessive talk and much noise, but the first is preferable.

The meaning is: do not raise your voices to a degree that exceeds the level reached by the voice of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The commentators said: the purpose of the verse is the glorification of the Prophet (ﷺ), his honouring, and that they should not call out to him as some of them call out to one another. ﴿And do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another﴾, that is: do not speak loudly when you address him, as you are accustomed to speaking loudly when one of you addresses another.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah commanded them to exalt His Prophet and to lower their voices, and to address him with tranquillity and dignity. It has also been said that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿and do not speak loudly to him﴾ is: do not say, "O Muhammad" or "O Ahmad," but say "O Prophet of Allah" or "O Messenger of Allah," out of honour for him. The *kāf* (in *ka-jahri*) is in the accusative position, as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning: loudly, like the loudness of some of you toward others.

What is meant by raising the voice and speaking loudly is not that which occurs in a manner of contempt, for that is disbelief (*kufr*). Rather, what is meant is that the voice itself is unsuitable for what occurs in the situations of one who must be venerated and honoured.

The summary is that the prohibition here concerns several matters. The first is going forward before him with speech he has not permitted. The second is raising the voice to a level that exceeds his voice, whether in addressing him or in addressing others. The third is abandoning rudeness in addressing him and adhering to good manners in his presence, because loud argument occurs only between equals, among whom none has a distinction over another that requires his respect and veneration.

Then He, glorified is He, gave the reason for what He mentioned in His saying: ﴿lest your deeds become worthless﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the estimated construction is *li-an taḥbaṭa a'mālukum* (in order that your deeds not become worthless), meaning *fa-taḥbaṭa* (so that they become worthless). The estimated *lām* is the *lām al-ṣayrūrah* (the *lām* of consequence), so he said. This reason may be taken as a reason for the prohibition, meaning: Allah forbade you from loud speech for fear that [your deeds] would become worthless, or out of dislike that they would become worthless. Or it is a reason for the forbidden act, meaning: do not do loud speech, for it leads to worthlessness. Thus al-Zajjaj's statement looks to the second aspect, not the first.

The clause ﴿while you do not perceive﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). In it is a severe warning and a great threat.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is not meant that the words "while you do not perceive" imply that a person may disbelieve while not knowing it. Just as a disbeliever does not become a believer except by his choosing faith over disbelief, likewise a disbeliever does not become a disbeliever through what he does not know.

Then He, glorified is He, encouraged compliance with what He commanded, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾. The root of *ghaḍḍ* is reduction from anything, and from it comes the reduction of the voice.

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* reported from her that she said: "Some people would precede Ramadan with a fast, that is, a day or two days. So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh also reported from her that "some people would precede the month and fast before the Prophet (ﷺ), so Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, the verse."

Al-Bazzar, Ibn 'Adi, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who said: "This verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, I will not speak to you except as a brother speaks in private conversation (al-sirar).'" In its chain (isnad) is Husayn ibn 'Umar, who is weak (da'if). However, it is supported by what 'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim narrated, and al-Hakim graded it sound (sahih), through the route of Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When this was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾, Abu Bakr said: 'By He who revealed the Book to you, O Messenger of Allah (p-1391), I will not speak to you except as a brother speaks in private conversation until I meet Allah.'"

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Anas, who said: "When this was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ up to His words ﴿while you do not perceive﴾, Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas had a loud voice. He said: 'I am the one who used to raise my voice over the voice of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). My deeds have been nullified, and I am among the people of the Fire.' He stayed in his house, grieving. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) missed him, so some of the people went to him and said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has missed you. What is wrong with you?' He said: 'I am the one who raises my voice above the voice of the Prophet and speaks loudly to him. My deeds have been nullified, and I am among the people of the Fire.' They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of this. He said: 'No, rather he is among the people of Paradise.' Then, on the day of Yamamah, he was killed."

There are hadiths with a similar meaning on this topic.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words ﴿Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾, "the verse," that he said: "It was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas." Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from Abu Hurayrah concerning His words: "﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Among them is Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas.'"

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: with a sound chain (sanad sahih), through the route of Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from al-Aqra' ibn Habis, that "he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, come out to us.' He did not respond to him. He said: 'O Muhammad, indeed my praise is an adornment and my blame is a disgrace.' He said: 'That is Allah.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who call you from behind the private chambers﴾."

Ibn Mani' said: "I do not know of any sound (musnad) narration from al-Aqra' other than this."

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good (hasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, "concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, those who call you from behind the private chambers﴾, he said: A man came and said: 'O Muhammad, indeed my praise is an adornment and my blame is a disgrace.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'That is Allah.'"

Ibn Rahawayh, Musaddad, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: with a good chain (isnad hasan), from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "A group of the Arabs gathered and said: 'Let us go to this man. If he is a prophet, then we are the happiest of people with him; and if he is a king, we will live under his wing.' I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of what they had said. They came to his chamber and began calling out: 'O Muhammad, O Muhammad!' Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who call you from behind the private chambers, most of them do not understand﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took my ear and began saying: 'Allah has certainly confirmed your statement, O Zayd. Allah has certainly confirmed your statement, O Zayd.'"

There are hadiths on this topic.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mandah and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: with a fine chain (isnad jayyid), from al-Harith ibn Dirar al-Khuza'i, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he invited me to Islam. I entered it and affirmed it, and he invited me to zakat, and I affirmed it. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I will return to my people and invite them to Islam and the payment of zakat. Whoever responds to me, I will gather his zakat, and you, O Messenger of Allah, should send a messenger to me at such-and-such an appointed time (al-iban), so that he may take what I have gathered of zakat.' When al-Harith had gathered the zakat from those who had responded to him, and the appointed time came that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had intended to send to him, the messenger was delayed and did not come. Al-Harith thought that some displeasure (sakhtah) from Allah and His Messenger had occurred concerning him. So he summoned the leaders of his people and said to them: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had set a time for me, when he would send his messenger to collect what I had of zakat. There is no breaking of promise from the Messenger of Allah, and I do not see the delay of his messenger except as a result of displeasure. So let us go and come to the Messenger of Allah.'

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah to al-Harith to collect what he had gathered of zakat. When al-Walid set out and reached part of the way, he became frightened and returned. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Al-Harith withheld zakat from me and intended to kill me.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dispatched a force (ba'th) to al-Harith. Al-Harith came with his companions, and when the force set out and departed from Madinah, al-Harith met them. They said: 'This is al-Harith?' When he approached them, he said to them: 'To whom have you been sent?' They said: 'To you.' He said: 'Why?' They said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah to you, and he claimed that you withheld zakat from him and intended to kill him.' He said: 'No, by He who sent Muhammad with the truth, I did not see him at all, and he did not come to me.' When al-Harith entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: 'Did you withhold zakat and intend to kill my messenger?' He said: 'No, by He who sent you with the truth, I did not see him, and he did not see me. I only came when the messenger of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was delayed for me, and I feared that there had been some displeasure from Allah and His Messenger.' Then this was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, if a dissolute person brings you news﴾ up to His words ﴿Wise﴾."

Ibn Kathir said: "This is among the finest of what has been narrated concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse."

Many narrations have been transmitted agreeing that it was the occasion of the revelation of the verse and that it is what is meant by it, even though the accounts differ.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 49, verses 1–8 (part 1 of 2)**

It is Madani (revealed at Medina). Al-Qurtubi said: by scholarly consensus (*ijma'*).

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr that it was revealed at Medina.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾. The majority of readers read *tuqaddimū* with a dammah on the *tā'* and a shaddah on the *dāl* with a kasrah. In it there are two possibilities. The first is that it is transitive, and its object has been omitted in order to generalize, or the object has been left out to focus on the verb itself, as in their saying: "He gives and withholds" (*huwa yu'ṭī wa-yamna'*).

The second is that it is intransitive, like *wajaha* and *tawajjaha*. This is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ya'qub, *taqaddamū* with a fatḥah on the *tā'*, the *qāf* and the *dāl*.

Al-Wahidi said: *qaddama* here has the meaning of *taqaddama*, and it is intransitive.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the Arabs say, "Do not go forward before the imam" and "before the father" (*lā taqaddam bayna yaday al-imām wa-bayna yaday al-āb*), meaning: do not act hastily in the matter without him, and do not forbid [anything] without him, because the meaning is: do not go forward before their command and their prohibition. "Before the imam" is an expression for the imam himself, not for what is in front of a person. The meaning of the verse is: do not cut off a matter apart from Allah and His Messenger, and do not hasten in it.

It has also been said that the intended sense of "before so-and-so" (*bayna yaday fulān*) is his presence, because whatever a person is present for is "before him." ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in all your affairs, and within this falls abandoning going forward before Allah and His Messenger, as a primary inclusion.

Then He gave the reason for the command to taqwā (God-consciousness) in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ of everything heard, ﴿Knowing﴾ of everything known.

﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾. It is possible that the intended meaning is the literal raising of the voice, because that indicates a lack of modesty and an abandonment of respect, since lowering the voice and not raising it is among the requirements of veneration and honour.

It is also possible that the intended meaning is a prohibition of excessive talk and much noise, but the first is preferable.

The meaning is: do not raise your voices to a degree that exceeds the level reached by the voice of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The commentators said: the purpose of the verse is the glorification of the Prophet (ﷺ), his honouring, and that they should not call out to him as some of them call out to one another. ﴿And do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another﴾, that is: do not speak loudly when you address him, as you are accustomed to speaking loudly when one of you addresses another.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah commanded them to exalt His Prophet and to lower their voices, and to address him with tranquillity and dignity. It has also been said that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿and do not speak loudly to him﴾ is: do not say, "O Muhammad" or "O Ahmad," but say "O Prophet of Allah" or "O Messenger of Allah," out of honour for him. The *kāf* (in *ka-jahri*) is in the accusative position, as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning: loudly, like the loudness of some of you toward others.

What is meant by raising the voice and speaking loudly is not that which occurs in a manner of contempt, for that is disbelief (*kufr*). Rather, what is meant is that the voice itself is unsuitable for what occurs in the situations of one who must be venerated and honoured.

The summary is that the prohibition here concerns several matters. The first is going forward before him with speech he has not permitted. The second is raising the voice to a level that exceeds his voice, whether in addressing him or in addressing others. The third is abandoning rudeness in addressing him and adhering to good manners in his presence, because loud argument occurs only between equals, among whom none has a distinction over another that requires his respect and veneration.

Then He, glorified is He, gave the reason for what He mentioned in His saying: ﴿lest your deeds become worthless﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the estimated construction is *li-an taḥbaṭa a'mālukum* (in order that your deeds not become worthless), meaning *fa-taḥbaṭa* (so that they become worthless). The estimated *lām* is the *lām al-ṣayrūrah* (the *lām* of consequence), so he said. This reason may be taken as a reason for the prohibition, meaning: Allah forbade you from loud speech for fear that [your deeds] would become worthless, or out of dislike that they would become worthless. Or it is a reason for the forbidden act, meaning: do not do loud speech, for it leads to worthlessness. Thus al-Zajjaj's statement looks to the second aspect, not the first.

The clause ﴿while you do not perceive﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). In it is a severe warning and a great threat.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is not meant that the words "while you do not perceive" imply that a person may disbelieve while not knowing it. Just as a disbeliever does not become a believer except by his choosing faith over disbelief, likewise a disbeliever does not become a disbeliever through what he does not know.

Then He, glorified is He, encouraged compliance with what He commanded, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾. The root of *ghaḍḍ* is reduction from anything, and from it comes the reduction of the voice.

﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾. Al-Farra' said: He sincerely purified their hearts for piety, as gold is tested by fire, so that its good is separated from its bad and its impurity falls away.

Muqatil, Mujahid and Qatada said the same.

Al-Akhfash said: He singled them out for piety. It has also been said: He purified them from every ugliness. And it has been said: He widened them and made them spacious, from *maḥantu al-adīm*, meaning when you stretch the hide.

Abu 'Amr said: everything you exert yourself in, you have *maḥantahu* (tested it).

The *lām* in ﴿for piety﴾ (*li-l-taqwā*) is connected to an omitted element, meaning: fit for piety, as when you say, "You are fit for such-and-such." Or it is the *lām* of causation functioning as an explanation of the cause, as when you say, "I came to you for the fulfilment of a duty," meaning: so that my coming would be the cause of the fulfilment of the duty.

﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾. That is: those, for them. So it is a second predicate of the demonstrative (*ism al-ishārah*). It is also possible that it is a new sentence explaining what Allah has prepared for them in the Hereafter.

﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers—most of them do not reason﴾. They are the rude people of the Banu Tamim, as its explanation will come. *Warā' al-ḥujurāt* means outside them and behind them. *Al-ḥujurāt* is the plural of *ḥujrah* (room), like *al-ghurufāt* the plural of *ghurfah* (upper room), and *al-ẓulumāt* the plural of *ẓulmah* (darkness). It has been said that *al-ḥujurāt* is the plural of *ḥujar*, and *ḥujar* is the plural of *ḥujrah*, so it is a plural of a plural. A *ḥujrah* is a piece of land enclosed by a wall that surrounds it, and it is of the pattern *faʿīlah* in the sense of *mafʿūlah*.

The majority read *al-ḥujurāt* with a ḍammah on the *jīm*. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and Shayba read it with a fatḥah, as a lightening. Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with a sukūn. These are dialectal variants. The *min* in *min warā'* indicates the starting point, and there is no reason to prevent taking it in this sense.

﴿Most of them do not reason﴾, because ignorance overpowers them and coarseness is abundant in their natures.

﴿And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾. That is: if they had waited for your emergence and had not hastened to call out, it would have been more righteous for them in their religion and their worldly affairs, because in that there is observance of good manners toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), protecting his noble status, and acting in accordance with the veneration and exaltation he deserves.

It has also been said: they came as intercessors concerning captives, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) freed half of them and ransomed half of them. Had they been patient, he would have freed all of them. Muqatil mentioned this meaning.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, abundant in forgiveness and mercy, and extreme in both. He does not hold such people to account for what they neglected of good manners.

﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you a report, verify it﴾. The majority read *fa-tabayyanū* from *tabayyun*, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *fa-tathabbatū* from *tathabbut*. What is meant by *tabayyun* is investigation and examination, and by *tathabbut* is deliberation, avoiding haste, and looking carefully into the matter that has occurred and the report that has arrived until it becomes clear and evident.

The commentators said: this verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, as its explanation will come, if Allah wills.

His saying ﴿lest you harm a people in ignorance﴾ is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*). That is: out of dislike that you harm, or lest you harm, or lest you harm because the error of one who has not verified the matter nor deliberated about it is the most common, and it is ignorance, because it did not proceed from knowledge. The meaning is: being involved in ignorance regarding their situation.

﴿And then you become, regarding what you have done﴾ to them by harming them through error, ﴿regretful﴾ over that, distressed by it and concerned with it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, admonished them, saying: ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah﴾. So do not say a false word, and do not rush when news reaches you without verification. The *anna* and what follows it fill the place of the two objects of *i'lamū* (know). The clause ﴿if he obeyed you in much of the matter, you would be in distress﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *fīkum* (among you), or it is a new sentence. The meaning: if he obeyed you in much of what you report to him of false news, and what you suggest to him of opinions that are not correct, you would fall into *'anat*, which is hardship, toil, sin and destruction. But he does not obey you in most of what you want before the clarity of its aspect becomes evident to him, and he does not hasten to act on what reaches him before considering it.

﴿But Allah has made faith beloved to you﴾, that is: He made it the most beloved of things to you, or made it loved by you, so that nothing proceeds from you except what agrees with it and requires righteous matters and abandoning haste in reports and not verifying them. It has been said: the intended meaning of "these" is those other than the first group, to clear them of the attributes of the first group. The apparent meaning is that it is a reminder to all of what faith requires and what the love that Allah placed in their hearts necessitates.

﴿And has made it beautiful in your hearts﴾, that is: made it good through His success, until they act according to what it requires in words and deeds.

﴿And has made disbelief, defiance and disobedience hateful to you﴾, that is: He made everything that is of the kind of defiance and of the kind of disobedience hateful in your sight.

The root of *fisq* is departure from obedience, and *iṣyān* is the category of what Allah is disobeyed by. It has been said: by this He meant specifically lying, but the first is preferable.

﴿Those are the rightly guided﴾, that is, those described by what they have been mentioned for. *Al-rushd* is steadfastness upon the path of truth with firmness, from *al-rashādah*, which is a rock.

﴿As a bounty from Allah and favour﴾, that is: for the sake of His bounty and grace. The meaning is that He made beloved to you what He made beloved, and made hateful to you what He made hateful, for the sake of His bounty and grace, or He made you rightly guided for that reason. It has been said: the accusative is by an estimated verb, meaning: you seek bounty and favour.

﴿And Allah is Knowing﴾ of everything known, ﴿Wise﴾ in everything He decrees among His servants and determines for them.

Al-Bukhari and others reported from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr who said: "A caravan of the Banu Tamim came to the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Bakr said, 'Appoint al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad,' and 'Umar said, 'Rather, appoint al-Aqra' ibn Habis.' Abu Bakr said, 'You only intended to oppose me.' 'Umar said, 'I did not intend to oppose you.' So they argued until their voices were raised, and Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ until the end of the verse."
