Al-Harith came with his companions, and when the force set out and departed from Madinah, al-Harith met them. They said: 'This is al-Harith?' When he approached them, he said to them: 'To whom have you been sent?' They said: 'To you.' He said: 'Why?' They said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah to you, and he claimed that you withheld zakat from him and intended to kill him.' He said: 'No, by He who sent Muhammad with the truth, I did not see him at all, and he did not come to me.' When al-Harith entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: 'Did you withhold zakat and intend to kill my messenger?' He said: 'No, by He who sent you with the truth, I did not see him, and he did not see me. I only came when the messenger of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was delayed for me, and I feared that there had been some displeasure from Allah and His Messenger.' Then this was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, if a dissolute person brings you news﴾ up to His words ﴿Wise﴾."

Ibn Kathir said: "This is among the finest of what has been narrated concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse."

Many narrations have been transmitted agreeing that it was the occasion of the revelation of the verse and that it is what is meant by it, even though the accounts differ.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 49, verses 9–12 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read *iqtatalu* (اقْتَتَلُوا) with the plural, taking into account each individual member of the two groups, as in His saying, ﴿These are two adversaries who dispute﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. The pronoun in His saying *baynahuma* (بَيْنَهُما, "between them") refers to the two groups, taking into account the wording.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read *iqtatalata* (اقْتَتَلَتا), taking into account the wording *taifatan* (طائِفَتانِ, "two groups"). Zayd ibn ʿAli and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read *iqtatala* (اقْتَتَلا), and the masculine verb in this reading is taking into account "the two parties" (al-fariqayn) or "the two companies" (al-rahtayn).

*Al-baghy* (البَغْيُ, transgression) is aggression without right, and refusing reconciliation that is in accordance with what is correct. *Al-fayʾ* (الفَيْءُ) is returning. The meaning is: if two groups of Muslims fight, the Muslims must strive for reconciliation between them and call them to the judgment of God. If, after that, one of the two groups commits aggression against the other and does not accept reconciliation nor enter into it, then the Muslims must fight this transgressing group until it returns to the command and judgment of God. If that transgressing group returns from its transgression and responds to the call to the Book of God and His judgment, then the Muslims must act justly between the two groups in judgment, seek out what is correct and in accordance with the judgment of God, and restrain the hand of the wrongdoing group until it leaves injustice and discharges what it owes to the other.

Then God, glorified is He, commanded the Muslims to act justly in all their affairs, after commanding them with this particular justice concerning the two fighting groups. He said, ﴿And act justly; indeed, God loves those who act justly﴾. That is: and be just, for God loves the just, and His love for them entails rewarding them with the best reward.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: ﴿So make reconciliation between them﴾ by calling them to the judgment of the Book of God and agreeing to what is in it, for them and against them. ﴿And if one of them transgresses against the other﴾ and seeks what is not its right and does not return to reconciliation, ﴿then fight the one that transgresses﴾ until it returns to the obedience of God and to the reconciliation that God has commanded.

The sentence ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ is a resumptive clause, confirming what precedes it of the command to reconciliation. The meaning is that they all go back to one origin, which is faith.

Al-Zajjaj said: Religion unites them, so they are brothers when they agree in their religion. They return by agreement in religion to the origin of lineage, since they all descend from Adam and Eve. ﴿So make reconciliation between your two brothers﴾ means every two Muslims who dispute and fight. The specification of two in mention is to establish the obligation of reconciliation for more than two by way of greater priority.

The majority read *bayna akhawaykum* (بَيْنَ أخَوَيْكم) in the dual. Zayd ibn Thabit, ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, al-Hasan, Hammad ibn Salamah and Ibn Sirin read *ikhwanikum* (إخْوانِكم) in the plural. It is reported from Abu ʿUmar, Nasr ibn ʿAsim, Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Jahdari and Yaʿqub that they read *bayna ikhwatikum* (بَيْنَ إخْوَتِكم) with the feminine-plural form, also in the plural.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi, in explaining the majority reading, said: He meant by the "two brothers" the two groups, because the dual form may be used and intend plurality.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: That is, make reconciliation between every two brothers. ﴿And fear God﴾ in all your affairs, ﴿that you may be shown mercy﴾ through piety. The expression of hope (*tarajji*, التَّرَجِّي) is with respect to those addressed, that is, hoping that you will be shown mercy.

In this verse is evidence for fighting the transgressing faction when its transgression is established against the imam or against any one of the Muslims. It also refutes the view of one who holds that fighting is not permissible, citing His saying (ﷺ): "Fighting a Muslim is disbelief." The intended meaning of this hadith and what has come in its sense is fighting a Muslim who does not transgress.

Ibn Jarir said: If the obligation, in every dispute that occurs between two groups of Muslims, were to flee from it and to remain in one's dwellings, then no right would be established and no falsehood would be annulled. The people of hypocrisy and immorality would find a means to make lawful everything that God has forbidden them: the wealth of the Muslims, the taking of their women captive, and the shedding of their blood, by forming factions against them, while the Muslims restrain their hands from them. This contradicts His saying (ﷺ): "Take hold of the hands of your foolish ones."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This verse is a foundation for fighting among Muslims and a principal reference in fighting those who interpret (the texts) in error. The Companions relied upon it, the notables of the religious community resorted to it, and it is what the Prophet (ﷺ) meant by his saying: "The transgressing faction will kill ʿAmmar." It is also what he (ﷺ) meant concerning the Kharijites: "They will come out at a time of division among the people, and the party nearer to the truth will kill them."

﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule another people, perhaps they are better than them﴾. *Al-sukhriyyah* (السُّخْرِيَةُ) is mockery, *al-istihza'* (الِاسْتِهْزاءُ). Abu Zayd reported: *sakhirtu bihi*, *dahiktu bihi* and *hazi'tu bihi* (I mocked him, I laughed at him, and I scoffed at him).

Al-Akhfash said: *sakhirtu minhu* and *sakhirtu bihi*, *dahiktu minhu* and *dahiktu bihi*, *hazi'tu minhu* and *hazi'tu bihi* are all said. The noun is *al-sukhriyyah* and *al-sukhra*, and both were read in His saying, ﴿that some of them may take others in service [sukhriyyan]﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32].

The meaning of the verse is a prohibition to the believers from one of them mocking another. He gave the reason for this prohibition with His saying, ﴿perhaps they are better than them﴾, that is, that the one being mocked may be better in the sight of God than those who mock him.

Since the word *qawm* (قَوْمٌ, "people") is specific to men, because they are the ones who take charge over women, He mentioned women separately, saying, ﴿nor women [of] women﴾, that is, let not women mock women, ﴿perhaps they are better than them﴾, meaning better than the women who mock them. It was said that He mentioned women separately because mockery among them is more frequent.

﴿And do not defame one another﴾. *Al-lamz* (اللَّمْزُ) is faultfinding. Its verification has already passed in Surah Bara'ah, at His saying, ﴿And among them are those who criticize you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58].

Ibn Jarir said: *Al-lamz* is by hand, eye, tongue and gesture, while *al-hamz* (الهَمْزُ) is only by tongue. The meaning of ﴿do not defame yourselves﴾ is that some of you should not defame others, as in His saying, ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29], and His saying, ﴿then greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61].

Mujahid, Qatadah and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: Let none of you slander another.

Al-Dahhak said: Let none of you curse another.

﴿And do not insult one another by [offensive] nicknames﴾. *Al-tanabuz* (التَّنابُزُ) is the reciprocal form from *al-nabz* (النَّبْزِ), with a sukun, which is the verbal noun, while *al-nabaz* (النَّبَزُ), with a fatha, is a nickname. Its plural is *anbaz*. *Al-alqab* (الألْقابُ) is the plural of *laqab* (لَقَبٌ), which is a name other than that by which a person was named. What is intended here is a bad nickname, and *al-tanabuz bil-alqab* is that some of them give nicknames to others.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: it is that one says to his Muslim brother, "O sinner! O hypocrite!", or says to one who has accepted Islam, "O Jew! O Christian!" ʿAta' said: It is everything by which you expel your brother from Islam, such as your saying, "O dog! O donkey! O pig!"

Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: A man would be reproached for his former disbelief, and it would be said to him, "O Jew! O Christian!" So this was revealed. Qatadah, Abu al-ʿAliyah and ʿIkrimah said the same.

﴿Wretched is the name of defiance after faith﴾. That is: wretched is the name by which they are mentioned with defiance (*fusuq*) after entering into faith. Here *al-ism* (الِاسْمُ, "name") has the sense of *al-dhikr* (الذِّكْرُ, "mention").

Ibn Zayd said: That is, wretched is it for a man to be named a disbeliever or an adulterer after his Islam and repentance.

It was also said that the meaning is: whoever does what is forbidden of mockery, defamation and nicknaming, then he is a defiant sinner.

Al-Qurtubi said: Excepted from this are those whose nicknames have become customary, such as "the lame" or "the hunchback," for whom there is no cause for resentment in one's soul. The scholars permitted this, and the people of the language agreed upon it. (End of quotation.)

﴿And whoever does not repent﴾ of what God has forbidden, ﴿those are the wrongdoers﴾, for committing what God forbade and refusing to repent. They wronged the one whom they nicknamed, and they wronged themselves by the sin that befell them.

(p-1393) ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of suspicion﴾. *Al-zann* (الظَّنُّ, "suspicion") here is mere accusation without any cause, like one who accuses another of some indecency when no sign of that has appeared on him. God, glorified is He, commanded avoidance of much of it, so that the believer examines every suspicion he holds until he knows its basis, because some suspicion must be followed. Most of the legal rulings are based on suspicion, such as analogy (*qiyas*, القِياسِ), the report of a single transmitter (*khabar al-wahid*, خَبَرِ الواحِدِ), and the indication of general wording (*dalalat al-ʿumum*, دَلالَةِ العُمُومِ). But this suspicion which must be acted upon has been strengthened by some means that makes acting upon it obligatory, so it rises above doubt and accusation.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is to suspect the people of goodness of evil. As for the people of evil and defiance, we may suspect them of the like of what has appeared from them.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: It is to suspect one's Muslim brother of evil, and there is no harm in it so long as one does not speak of it. If he speaks of that suspicion and reveals it, he sins.

Al-Qurtubi reported from most scholars that a bad suspicion of one whose outward state is good is not permissible, and that there is no blame in a bad suspicion of one whose outward state is bad. His saying, ﴿Indeed, some suspicion is sin﴾, is a justification for what precedes it, the command to avoid much suspicion. This "some" is the suspicion of evil about the people of goodness, and the sin is the punishment that the one who suspects deserves.

Among what indicates that this suspicion which is commanded to be avoided is restricted to suspicion of evil is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And you assumed an assumption of evil, and you were a people ruined﴾ [al-Fath: 12]. Therefore, nothing of the suspicion that is commanded to be followed in matters of religion enters into the suspicion commanded to be avoided, for God has made His servants worship by following it, and most scholars have held it obligatory to act upon it. None denied this except some sects of innovators, out of hostility to the religion and deviation from the majority of Muslims. The worship through suspicion has come in much of the purified Law, indeed in most of it.

Then, when God, glorified is He, commanded them to avoid much suspicion, He forbade them from spying, saying, ﴿And do not spy﴾. *Al-tajassus* (التَّجَسُّسُ) is searching for what is concealed from you of the faults and private matters of the Muslims. God, glorified is He, forbade them from searching for people's defects and shortcomings.

The majority read ﴿tajassasu﴾ with the *jim* (بِالجِيمِ), and its meaning is what we have mentioned. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Ibn Sirin read it with the *ha'* (بِالحاءِ).

Al-Akhfash said: Neither of them is far from the other, because *tajassus* with the *jim* is searching for what is concealed from you, and *tahassus* with the *ha'* is seeking news and searching for it.

It was also said: *tajassus* with the *jim* is searching, and from it comes the saying "a man is a *jasus*" (spy) when he searches out affairs. With the *ha'* it is what a person perceives through some of his senses.

It was said: with the *ha'* it is what a person seeks for himself, and with the *jim* it is to act as a messenger for another. This was said by Tha'lab.

﴿And let not some of you backbite others﴾. That is: let not some of you speak of others in their absence with what would displease them. *Al-ghibah* (الغِيبَةُ, backbiting) is that you mention a man with what he dislikes, as in the hadith of Abu Hurairah, established in the Sahih, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do you know what backbiting is?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "Your mentioning your brother with what he dislikes." It was said: "What if what I say is true of my brother?" He said: "If what you say is in him, then you have backbitten him, and if it is not in him, then you have slandered him."

﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾ He, glorified is He, likened backbiting to eating carrion, because the dead person does not know that his flesh is being eaten, just as the living person does not know of the backbiting done about him. Al-Zajjaj mentioned this meaning.

This passage contains an indication that a person's honour is like his flesh: just as eating his flesh is forbidden, so is overstepping against his honour. There is, in this, a warning against backbiting (al-ghība), a rebuke to the one who commits it, and a strong condemnation of him, which is clear. Human nature recoils from eating human flesh, and the human disposition finds it repugnant, quite apart from its being forbidden by the Law. Thus ﴿فَكَرِهْتُمُوهُ﴾ ("so you have disliked it"). Al-Farra' said: "Its implied reading is: ﴿فَقَدْ كَرِهْتُمُوهُ﴾ ('so you have indeed disliked it'), so do not do it." The meaning is: just as you dislike this, avoid mentioning your brother with evil in his absence. Al-Razi said: "The fa' (so) is in the sense of a response to a statement, as if he had said: 'None of you would love to eat the flesh of his brother; so you have disliked it, then.'"

Abu al-Baqa' said: "It is coordinated with an omitted element, its implied meaning being: 'This was presented to you, so you disliked it.'" ﴿وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ﴾ ("And fear Allah") by abandoning what He has commanded you to avoid. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ تَوَّابٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance, Merciful") toward whoever fears Him, for what has passed from him of sin and of opposing the command.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from Anas, who said: It was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If only you would visit Abdullah ibn Ubayy." So he set off to him, riding a donkey, and the Muslims set out walking, and the land was salty (sabakha). When he reached him, [Abdullah] said: "Keep away from me! By Allah, the smell of your donkey has harmed me." A man from the Ansar said: "By Allah, the donkey of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is better in smell than you!" Then men from his people became angry on behalf of Abdullah, and his companions became angry on behalf of each of them, so there was striking between them with palm-stalks, with hands and with sandals. Then there was revealed concerning them: ﴿وَإِن طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ ("And if two groups of the believers fight...") and so on.

Something similar has been related through other channels.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn Umar, who said: "I have not felt anything in myself as much as I felt about this verse: that I did not fight this rebellious group as Allah commanded me."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning the verse, who said: Allah commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers that when a group of believers fights, they should call them to the judgement of Allah and do justice between them. If they respond, he judges among them by the judgement of the Book of Allah until the wronged one is given justice. Whoever refuses to respond among them is a rebel (baghin), and it is incumbent upon the leader (imam) of the believers and the believers to fight them until they return to the command of Allah and acknowledge the judgement of Allah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿وَإِن طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ ("And if two groups of the believers fight..."), who said: There was fighting with sandals and staves, so He commanded them to reconcile between the two.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Aisha, who said: "I have not seen anything like what this nation has turned away from in this verse: ﴿وَإِن طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا فَأَصْلِحُوا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ ('And if two groups of the believers fight, then make reconciliation between them')."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muqatil concerning His saying: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا يَسْخَرْ قَوْمٌ مِّن قَوْمٍ﴾ ("O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people") that he said: It was revealed concerning a people from Banu Tamim who mocked Bilal, Salman, Ammar, Khabbab, Suhayb, Ibn Fuhayra and Salim, the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa.

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Dhamm al-Ghiba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَلْمِزُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ﴾ ("And do not defame one another") that he said: Let none of you slander another.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, the authors of the Four Sunan, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, transmitted from Abu Jabira ibn al-Dahhak, who said: "It was revealed concerning us, the Banu Salama: ﴿وَلَا تَنَابَزُوا بِالْأَلْقَابِ﴾ ('And do not insult one another by nicknames'). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came, and there was not a man among us except that he had two or three names. Whenever he called one of them by one of those names, they would say: 'O Messenger of Allah, he dislikes it!' So there was revealed: ﴿وَلَا تَنَابَزُوا بِالْأَلْقَابِ﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted something similar from Ibn Abbas.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: Mutual insulting by nicknames is that a man has committed evil deeds, then repented of them and returned to the truth, and Allah forbade that he be reproached for what had preceded from his deeds.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse, who said: If a man was a Jew and then embraced Islam, and [another] would say to him: "O Jew! O Christian! O Magian!", and would say to a Muslim man: "O sinner (fasiq)!"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اجْتَنِبُوا كَثِيرًا مِّنَ الظَّنِّ﴾ ("O you who have believed, avoid much of suspicion"), who said: Allah forbade the believer to suspect ill of a believer.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most false of speech. Do not spy, do not seek out secrets, do not compete one with another, do not envy one another, do not hate one another, and be servants of Allah as brothers. A man should not make an offer upon the offer of his brother until he marries or leaves [the matter]."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا﴾ ("And do not spy"), who said: Allah forbade the believer to pursue the faults (awrat) of a believer.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Zayd ibn Wahb, who said: Ibn Mas'ud was brought word, and it was said: "This is so-and-so, whose beard is dripping with wine!" Ibn Mas'ud said: "We have indeed been forbidden to spy, but if something becomes apparent to us, we will take it."

Traditions have also come down forbidding the pursuit of the faults of Muslims and spying upon their defects.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿وَلَا يَغْتَب بَّعْضُكُم بَعْضًا﴾ ("And let not some of you backbite others") to the end of the verse, who said: Allah has forbidden that a believer be backbitten about anything, just as He forbade carrion.

The traditions on the prohibition of backbiting are very numerous and well known in the books of hadith.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 49, verses 9–12 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read *iqtatalu* (اقْتَتَلُوا) with the plural, taking into account each individual member of the two groups, as in His saying, ﴿These are two adversaries who dispute﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. The pronoun in His saying *baynahuma* (بَيْنَهُما, "between them") refers to the two groups, taking into account the wording.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read *iqtatalata* (اقْتَتَلَتا), taking into account the wording *taifatan* (طائِفَتانِ, "two groups"). Zayd ibn ʿAli and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read *iqtatala* (اقْتَتَلا), and the masculine verb in this reading is taking into account "the two parties" (al-fariqayn) or "the two companies" (al-rahtayn).

*Al-baghy* (البَغْيُ, transgression) is aggression without right, and refusing reconciliation that is in accordance with what is correct. *Al-fayʾ* (الفَيْءُ) is returning. The meaning is: if two groups of Muslims fight, the Muslims must strive for reconciliation between them and call them to the judgment of God. If, after that, one of the two groups commits aggression against the other and does not accept reconciliation nor enter into it, then the Muslims must fight this transgressing group until it returns to the command and judgment of God. If that transgressing group returns from its transgression and responds to the call to the Book of God and His judgment, then the Muslims must act justly between the two groups in judgment, seek out what is correct and in accordance with the judgment of God, and restrain the hand of the wrongdoing group until it leaves injustice and discharges what it owes to the other.

Then God, glorified is He, commanded the Muslims to act justly in all their affairs, after commanding them with this particular justice concerning the two fighting groups. He said, ﴿And act justly; indeed, God loves those who act justly﴾. That is: and be just, for God loves the just, and His love for them entails rewarding them with the best reward.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: ﴿So make reconciliation between them﴾ by calling them to the judgment of the Book of God and agreeing to what is in it, for them and against them. ﴿And if one of them transgresses against the other﴾ and seeks what is not its right and does not return to reconciliation, ﴿then fight the one that transgresses﴾ until it returns to the obedience of God and to the reconciliation that God has commanded.

The sentence ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ is a resumptive clause, confirming what precedes it of the command to reconciliation. The meaning is that they all go back to one origin, which is faith.

Al-Zajjaj said: Religion unites them, so they are brothers when they agree in their religion. They return by agreement in religion to the origin of lineage, since they all descend from Adam and Eve. ﴿So make reconciliation between your two brothers﴾ means every two Muslims who dispute and fight. The specification of two in mention is to establish the obligation of reconciliation for more than two by way of greater priority.

The majority read *bayna akhawaykum* (بَيْنَ أخَوَيْكم) in the dual. Zayd ibn Thabit, ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, al-Hasan, Hammad ibn Salamah and Ibn Sirin read *ikhwanikum* (إخْوانِكم) in the plural. It is reported from Abu ʿUmar, Nasr ibn ʿAsim, Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Jahdari and Yaʿqub that they read *bayna ikhwatikum* (بَيْنَ إخْوَتِكم) with the feminine-plural form, also in the plural.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi, in explaining the majority reading, said: He meant by the "two brothers" the two groups, because the dual form may be used and intend plurality.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: That is, make reconciliation between every two brothers. ﴿And fear God﴾ in all your affairs, ﴿that you may be shown mercy﴾ through piety. The expression of hope (*tarajji*, التَّرَجِّي) is with respect to those addressed, that is, hoping that you will be shown mercy.

In this verse is evidence for fighting the transgressing faction when its transgression is established against the imam or against any one of the Muslims. It also refutes the view of one who holds that fighting is not permissible, citing His saying (ﷺ): "Fighting a Muslim is disbelief." The intended meaning of this hadith and what has come in its sense is fighting a Muslim who does not transgress.

Ibn Jarir said: If the obligation, in every dispute that occurs between two groups of Muslims, were to flee from it and to remain in one's dwellings, then no right would be established and no falsehood would be annulled. The people of hypocrisy and immorality would find a means to make lawful everything that God has forbidden them: the wealth of the Muslims, the taking of their women captive, and the shedding of their blood, by forming factions against them, while the Muslims restrain their hands from them. This contradicts His saying (ﷺ): "Take hold of the hands of your foolish ones."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This verse is a foundation for fighting among Muslims and a principal reference in fighting those who interpret (the texts) in error. The Companions relied upon it, the notables of the religious community resorted to it, and it is what the Prophet (ﷺ) meant by his saying: "The transgressing faction will kill ʿAmmar." It is also what he (ﷺ) meant concerning the Kharijites: "They will come out at a time of division among the people, and the party nearer to the truth will kill them."

﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule another people, perhaps they are better than them﴾. *Al-sukhriyyah* (السُّخْرِيَةُ) is mockery, *al-istihza'* (الِاسْتِهْزاءُ). Abu Zayd reported: *sakhirtu bihi*, *dahiktu bihi* and *hazi'tu bihi* (I mocked him, I laughed at him, and I scoffed at him).

Al-Akhfash said: *sakhirtu minhu* and *sakhirtu bihi*, *dahiktu minhu* and *dahiktu bihi*, *hazi'tu minhu* and *hazi'tu bihi* are all said. The noun is *al-sukhriyyah* and *al-sukhra*, and both were read in His saying, ﴿that some of them may take others in service [sukhriyyan]﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32].

The meaning of the verse is a prohibition to the believers from one of them mocking another. He gave the reason for this prohibition with His saying, ﴿perhaps they are better than them﴾, that is, that the one being mocked may be better in the sight of God than those who mock him.

Since the word *qawm* (قَوْمٌ, "people") is specific to men, because they are the ones who take charge over women, He mentioned women separately, saying, ﴿nor women [of] women﴾, that is, let not women mock women, ﴿perhaps they are better than them﴾, meaning better than the women who mock them. It was said that He mentioned women separately because mockery among them is more frequent.

﴿And do not defame one another﴾. *Al-lamz* (اللَّمْزُ) is faultfinding. Its verification has already passed in Surah Bara'ah, at His saying, ﴿And among them are those who criticize you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58].

Ibn Jarir said: *Al-lamz* is by hand, eye, tongue and gesture, while *al-hamz* (الهَمْزُ) is only by tongue. The meaning of ﴿do not defame yourselves﴾ is that some of you should not defame others, as in His saying, ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29], and His saying, ﴿then greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61].

Mujahid, Qatadah and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: Let none of you slander another.

Al-Dahhak said: Let none of you curse another.

﴿And do not insult one another by [offensive] nicknames﴾. *Al-tanabuz* (التَّنابُزُ) is the reciprocal form from *al-nabz* (النَّبْزِ), with a sukun, which is the verbal noun, while *al-nabaz* (النَّبَزُ), with a fatha, is a nickname. Its plural is *anbaz*. *Al-alqab* (الألْقابُ) is the plural of *laqab* (لَقَبٌ), which is a name other than that by which a person was named. What is intended here is a bad nickname, and *al-tanabuz bil-alqab* is that some of them give nicknames to others.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: it is that one says to his Muslim brother, "O sinner! O hypocrite!", or says to one who has accepted Islam, "O Jew! O Christian!" ʿAta' said: It is everything by which you expel your brother from Islam, such as your saying, "O dog! O donkey! O pig!"

Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: A man would be reproached for his former disbelief, and it would be said to him, "O Jew! O Christian!" So this was revealed. Qatadah, Abu al-ʿAliyah and ʿIkrimah said the same.

﴿Wretched is the name of defiance after faith﴾. That is: wretched is the name by which they are mentioned with defiance (*fusuq*) after entering into faith. Here *al-ism* (الِاسْمُ, "name") has the sense of *al-dhikr* (الذِّكْرُ, "mention").

Ibn Zayd said: That is, wretched is it for a man to be named a disbeliever or an adulterer after his Islam and repentance.

It was also said that the meaning is: whoever does what is forbidden of mockery, defamation and nicknaming, then he is a defiant sinner.

Al-Qurtubi said: Excepted from this are those whose nicknames have become customary, such as "the lame" or "the hunchback," for whom there is no cause for resentment in one's soul. The scholars permitted this, and the people of the language agreed upon it. (End of quotation.)

﴿And whoever does not repent﴾ of what God has forbidden, ﴿those are the wrongdoers﴾, for committing what God forbade and refusing to repent. They wronged the one whom they nicknamed, and they wronged themselves by the sin that befell them.

(p-1393) ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of suspicion﴾. *Al-zann* (الظَّنُّ, "suspicion") here is mere accusation without any cause, like one who accuses another of some indecency when no sign of that has appeared on him. God, glorified is He, commanded avoidance of much of it, so that the believer examines every suspicion he holds until he knows its basis, because some suspicion must be followed. Most of the legal rulings are based on suspicion, such as analogy (*qiyas*, القِياسِ), the report of a single transmitter (*khabar al-wahid*, خَبَرِ الواحِدِ), and the indication of general wording (*dalalat al-ʿumum*, دَلالَةِ العُمُومِ). But this suspicion which must be acted upon has been strengthened by some means that makes acting upon it obligatory, so it rises above doubt and accusation.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is to suspect the people of goodness of evil. As for the people of evil and defiance, we may suspect them of the like of what has appeared from them.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: It is to suspect one's Muslim brother of evil, and there is no harm in it so long as one does not speak of it. If he speaks of that suspicion and reveals it, he sins.

Al-Qurtubi reported from most scholars that a bad suspicion of one whose outward state is good is not permissible, and that there is no blame in a bad suspicion of one whose outward state is bad. His saying, ﴿Indeed, some suspicion is sin﴾, is a justification for what precedes it, the command to avoid much suspicion. This "some" is the suspicion of evil about the people of goodness, and the sin is the punishment that the one who suspects deserves.

Among what indicates that this suspicion which is commanded to be avoided is restricted to suspicion of evil is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And you assumed an assumption of evil, and you were a people ruined﴾ [al-Fath: 12]. Therefore, nothing of the suspicion that is commanded to be followed in matters of religion enters into the suspicion commanded to be avoided, for God has made His servants worship by following it, and most scholars have held it obligatory to act upon it. None denied this except some sects of innovators, out of hostility to the religion and deviation from the majority of Muslims. The worship through suspicion has come in much of the purified Law, indeed in most of it.

Then, when God, glorified is He, commanded them to avoid much suspicion, He forbade them from spying, saying, ﴿And do not spy﴾. *Al-tajassus* (التَّجَسُّسُ) is searching for what is concealed from you of the faults and private matters of the Muslims. God, glorified is He, forbade them from searching for people's defects and shortcomings.

The majority read ﴿tajassasu﴾ with the *jim* (بِالجِيمِ), and its meaning is what we have mentioned. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Ibn Sirin read it with the *ha'* (بِالحاءِ).

Al-Akhfash said: Neither of them is far from the other, because *tajassus* with the *jim* is searching for what is concealed from you, and *tahassus* with the *ha'* is seeking news and searching for it.

It was also said: *tajassus* with the *jim* is searching, and from it comes the saying "a man is a *jasus*" (spy) when he searches out affairs. With the *ha'* it is what a person perceives through some of his senses.

It was said: with the *ha'* it is what a person seeks for himself, and with the *jim* it is to act as a messenger for another. This was said by Tha'lab.

﴿And let not some of you backbite others﴾. That is: let not some of you speak of others in their absence with what would displease them. *Al-ghibah* (الغِيبَةُ, backbiting) is that you mention a man with what he dislikes, as in the hadith of Abu Hurairah, established in the Sahih, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do you know what backbiting is?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "Your mentioning your brother with what he dislikes." It was said: "What if what I say is true of my brother?" He said: "If what you say is in him, then you have backbitten him, and if it is not in him, then you have slandered him."

﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾ He, glorified is He, likened backbiting to eating carrion, because the dead person does not know that his flesh is being eaten, just as the living person does not know of the backbiting done about him. Al-Zajjaj mentioned this meaning.

This passage contains an indication that a person's honour is like his flesh: just as eating his flesh is forbidden, so is overstepping against his honour. There is, in this, a warning against backbiting (al-ghība), a rebuke to the one who commits it, and a strong condemnation of him, which is clear. Human nature recoils from eating human flesh, and the human disposition finds it repugnant, quite apart from its being forbidden by the Law. Thus ﴿فَكَرِهْتُمُوهُ﴾ ("so you have disliked it"). Al-Farra' said: "Its implied reading is: ﴿فَقَدْ كَرِهْتُمُوهُ﴾ ('so you have indeed disliked it'), so do not do it." The meaning is: just as you dislike this, avoid mentioning your brother with evil in his absence. Al-Razi said: "The fa' (so) is in the sense of a response to a statement, as if he had said: 'None of you would love to eat the flesh of his brother; so you have disliked it, then.'"

Abu al-Baqa' said: "It is coordinated with an omitted element, its implied meaning being: 'This was presented to you, so you disliked it.'" ﴿وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ﴾ ("And fear Allah") by abandoning what He has commanded you to avoid. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ تَوَّابٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance, Merciful") toward whoever fears Him, for what has passed from him of sin and of opposing the command.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from Anas, who said: It was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If only you would visit Abdullah ibn Ubayy." So he set off to him, riding a donkey, and the Muslims set out walking, and the land was salty (sabakha). When he reached him, [Abdullah] said: "Keep away from me! By Allah, the smell of your donkey has harmed me." A man from the Ansar said: "By Allah, the donkey of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is better in smell than you!" Then men from his people became angry on behalf of Abdullah, and his companions became angry on behalf of each of them, so there was striking between them with palm-stalks, with hands and with sandals. Then there was revealed concerning them: ﴿وَإِن طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ ("And if two groups of the believers fight...") and so on.

Something similar has been related through other channels.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn Umar, who said: "I have not felt anything in myself as much as I felt about this verse: that I did not fight this rebellious group as Allah commanded me."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning the verse, who said: Allah commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers that when a group of believers fights, they should call them to the judgement of Allah and do justice between them. If they respond, he judges among them by the judgement of the Book of Allah until the wronged one is given justice. Whoever refuses to respond among them is a rebel (baghin), and it is incumbent upon the leader (imam) of the believers and the believers to fight them until they return to the command of Allah and acknowledge the judgement of Allah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿وَإِن طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ ("And if two groups of the believers fight..."), who said: There was fighting with sandals and staves, so He commanded them to reconcile between the two.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Aisha, who said: "I have not seen anything like what this nation has turned away from in this verse: ﴿وَإِن طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا فَأَصْلِحُوا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ ('And if two groups of the believers fight, then make reconciliation between them')."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muqatil concerning His saying: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا يَسْخَرْ قَوْمٌ مِّن قَوْمٍ﴾ ("O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people") that he said: It was revealed concerning a people from Banu Tamim who mocked Bilal, Salman, Ammar, Khabbab, Suhayb, Ibn Fuhayra and Salim, the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa.

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Dhamm al-Ghiba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَلْمِزُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ﴾ ("And do not defame one another") that he said: Let none of you slander another.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, the authors of the Four Sunan, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, transmitted from Abu Jabira ibn al-Dahhak, who said: "It was revealed concerning us, the Banu Salama: ﴿وَلَا تَنَابَزُوا بِالْأَلْقَابِ﴾ ('And do not insult one another by nicknames'). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came, and there was not a man among us except that he had two or three names. Whenever he called one of them by one of those names, they would say: 'O Messenger of Allah, he dislikes it!' So there was revealed: ﴿وَلَا تَنَابَزُوا بِالْأَلْقَابِ﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted something similar from Ibn Abbas.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: Mutual insulting by nicknames is that a man has committed evil deeds, then repented of them and returned to the truth, and Allah forbade that he be reproached for what had preceded from his deeds.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse, who said: If a man was a Jew and then embraced Islam, and [another] would say to him: "O Jew! O Christian! O Magian!", and would say to a Muslim man: "O sinner (fasiq)!"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اجْتَنِبُوا كَثِيرًا مِّنَ الظَّنِّ﴾ ("O you who have believed, avoid much of suspicion"), who said: Allah forbade the believer to suspect ill of a believer.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most false of speech. Do not spy, do not seek out secrets, do not compete one with another, do not envy one another, do not hate one another, and be servants of Allah as brothers. A man should not make an offer upon the offer of his brother until he marries or leaves [the matter]."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا﴾ ("And do not spy"), who said: Allah forbade the believer to pursue the faults (awrat) of a believer.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Zayd ibn Wahb, who said: Ibn Mas'ud was brought word, and it was said: "This is so-and-so, whose beard is dripping with wine!" Ibn Mas'ud said: "We have indeed been forbidden to spy, but if something becomes apparent to us, we will take it."

Traditions have also come down forbidding the pursuit of the faults of Muslims and spying upon their defects.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿وَلَا يَغْتَب بَّعْضُكُم بَعْضًا﴾ ("And let not some of you backbite others") to the end of the verse, who said: Allah has forbidden that a believer be backbitten about anything, just as He forbade carrion.

The traditions on the prohibition of backbiting are very numerous and well known in the books of hadith.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 49, verses 9–12 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read *iqtatalu* (اقْتَتَلُوا) with the plural, taking into account each individual member of the two groups, as in His saying, ﴿These are two adversaries who dispute﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. The pronoun in His saying *baynahuma* (بَيْنَهُما, "between them") refers to the two groups, taking into account the wording.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read *iqtatalata* (اقْتَتَلَتا), taking into account the wording *taifatan* (طائِفَتانِ, "two groups"). Zayd ibn ʿAli and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read *iqtatala* (اقْتَتَلا), and the masculine verb in this reading is taking into account "the two parties" (al-fariqayn) or "the two companies" (al-rahtayn).

*Al-baghy* (البَغْيُ, transgression) is aggression without right, and refusing reconciliation that is in accordance with what is correct. *Al-fayʾ* (الفَيْءُ) is returning. The meaning is: if two groups of Muslims fight, the Muslims must strive for reconciliation between them and call them to the judgment of God. If, after that, one of the two groups commits aggression against the other and does not accept reconciliation nor enter into it, then the Muslims must fight this transgressing group until it returns to the command and judgment of God. If that transgressing group returns from its transgression and responds to the call to the Book of God and His judgment, then the Muslims must act justly between the two groups in judgment, seek out what is correct and in accordance with the judgment of God, and restrain the hand of the wrongdoing group until it leaves injustice and discharges what it owes to the other.

Then God, glorified is He, commanded the Muslims to act justly in all their affairs, after commanding them with this particular justice concerning the two fighting groups. He said, ﴿And act justly; indeed, God loves those who act justly﴾. That is: and be just, for God loves the just, and His love for them entails rewarding them with the best reward.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: ﴿So make reconciliation between them﴾ by calling them to the judgment of the Book of God and agreeing to what is in it, for them and against them. ﴿And if one of them transgresses against the other﴾ and seeks what is not its right and does not return to reconciliation, ﴿then fight the one that transgresses﴾ until it returns to the obedience of God and to the reconciliation that God has commanded.

The sentence ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ is a resumptive clause, confirming what precedes it of the command to reconciliation. The meaning is that they all go back to one origin, which is faith.

Al-Zajjaj said: Religion unites them, so they are brothers when they agree in their religion. They return by agreement in religion to the origin of lineage, since they all descend from Adam and Eve. ﴿So make reconciliation between your two brothers﴾ means every two Muslims who dispute and fight. The specification of two in mention is to establish the obligation of reconciliation for more than two by way of greater priority.

The majority read *bayna akhawaykum* (بَيْنَ أخَوَيْكم) in the dual. Zayd ibn Thabit, ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, al-Hasan, Hammad ibn Salamah and Ibn Sirin read *ikhwanikum* (إخْوانِكم) in the plural. It is reported from Abu ʿUmar, Nasr ibn ʿAsim, Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Jahdari and Yaʿqub that they read *bayna ikhwatikum* (بَيْنَ إخْوَتِكم) with the feminine-plural form, also in the plural.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi, in explaining the majority reading, said: He meant by the "two brothers" the two groups, because the dual form may be used and intend plurality.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: That is, make reconciliation between every two brothers. ﴿And fear God﴾ in all your affairs, ﴿that you may be shown mercy﴾ through piety. The expression of hope (*tarajji*, التَّرَجِّي) is with respect to those addressed, that is, hoping that you will be shown mercy.

In this verse is evidence for fighting the transgressing faction when its transgression is established against the imam or against any one of the Muslims. It also refutes the view of one who holds that fighting is not permissible, citing His saying (ﷺ): "Fighting a Muslim is disbelief." The intended meaning of this hadith and what has come in its sense is fighting a Muslim who does not transgress.

Ibn Jarir said: If the obligation, in every dispute that occurs between two groups of Muslims, were to flee from it and to remain in one's dwellings, then no right would be established and no falsehood would be annulled. The people of hypocrisy and immorality would find a means to make lawful everything that God has forbidden them: the wealth of the Muslims, the taking of their women captive, and the shedding of their blood, by forming factions against them, while the Muslims restrain their hands from them. This contradicts His saying (ﷺ): "Take hold of the hands of your foolish ones."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This verse is a foundation for fighting among Muslims and a principal reference in fighting those who interpret (the texts) in error. The Companions relied upon it, the notables of the religious community resorted to it, and it is what the Prophet (ﷺ) meant by his saying: "The transgressing faction will kill ʿAmmar." It is also what he (ﷺ) meant concerning the Kharijites: "They will come out at a time of division among the people, and the party nearer to the truth will kill them."

﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule another people, perhaps they are better than them﴾. *Al-sukhriyyah* (السُّخْرِيَةُ) is mockery, *al-istihza'* (الِاسْتِهْزاءُ). Abu Zayd reported: *sakhirtu bihi*, *dahiktu bihi* and *hazi'tu bihi* (I mocked him, I laughed at him, and I scoffed at him).

Al-Akhfash said: *sakhirtu minhu* and *sakhirtu bihi*, *dahiktu minhu* and *dahiktu bihi*, *hazi'tu minhu* and *hazi'tu bihi* are all said. The noun is *al-sukhriyyah* and *al-sukhra*, and both were read in His saying, ﴿that some of them may take others in service [sukhriyyan]﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32].

The meaning of the verse is a prohibition to the believers from one of them mocking another. He gave the reason for this prohibition with His saying, ﴿perhaps they are better than them﴾, that is, that the one being mocked may be better in the sight of God than those who mock him.

Since the word *qawm* (قَوْمٌ, "people") is specific to men, because they are the ones who take charge over women, He mentioned women separately, saying, ﴿nor women [of] women﴾, that is, let not women mock women, ﴿perhaps they are better than them﴾, meaning better than the women who mock them. It was said that He mentioned women separately because mockery among them is more frequent.

﴿And do not defame one another﴾. *Al-lamz* (اللَّمْزُ) is faultfinding. Its verification has already passed in Surah Bara'ah, at His saying, ﴿And among them are those who criticize you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58].

Ibn Jarir said: *Al-lamz* is by hand, eye, tongue and gesture, while *al-hamz* (الهَمْزُ) is only by tongue. The meaning of ﴿do not defame yourselves﴾ is that some of you should not defame others, as in His saying, ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29], and His saying, ﴿then greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61].

Mujahid, Qatadah and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: Let none of you slander another.

Al-Dahhak said: Let none of you curse another.

﴿And do not insult one another by [offensive] nicknames﴾. *Al-tanabuz* (التَّنابُزُ) is the reciprocal form from *al-nabz* (النَّبْزِ), with a sukun, which is the verbal noun, while *al-nabaz* (النَّبَزُ), with a fatha, is a nickname. Its plural is *anbaz*. *Al-alqab* (الألْقابُ) is the plural of *laqab* (لَقَبٌ), which is a name other than that by which a person was named. What is intended here is a bad nickname, and *al-tanabuz bil-alqab* is that some of them give nicknames to others.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: it is that one says to his Muslim brother, "O sinner! O hypocrite!", or says to one who has accepted Islam, "O Jew! O Christian!" ʿAta' said: It is everything by which you expel your brother from Islam, such as your saying, "O dog! O donkey! O pig!"

Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: A man would be reproached for his former disbelief, and it would be said to him, "O Jew! O Christian!" So this was revealed. Qatadah, Abu al-ʿAliyah and ʿIkrimah said the same.

﴿Wretched is the name of defiance after faith﴾. That is: wretched is the name by which they are mentioned with defiance (*fusuq*) after entering into faith. Here *al-ism* (الِاسْمُ, "name") has the sense of *al-dhikr* (الذِّكْرُ, "mention").

Ibn Zayd said: That is, wretched is it for a man to be named a disbeliever or an adulterer after his Islam and repentance.

It was also said that the meaning is: whoever does what is forbidden of mockery, defamation and nicknaming, then he is a defiant sinner.

Al-Qurtubi said: Excepted from this are those whose nicknames have become customary, such as "the lame" or "the hunchback," for whom there is no cause for resentment in one's soul. The scholars permitted this, and the people of the language agreed upon it. (End of quotation.)

﴿And whoever does not repent﴾ of what God has forbidden, ﴿those are the wrongdoers﴾, for committing what God forbade and refusing to repent. They wronged the one whom they nicknamed, and they wronged themselves by the sin that befell them.

(p-1393) ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of suspicion﴾. *Al-zann* (الظَّنُّ, "suspicion") here is mere accusation without any cause, like one who accuses another of some indecency when no sign of that has appeared on him. God, glorified is He, commanded avoidance of much of it, so that the believer examines every suspicion he holds until he knows its basis, because some suspicion must be followed. Most of the legal rulings are based on suspicion, such as analogy (*qiyas*, القِياسِ), the report of a single transmitter (*khabar al-wahid*, خَبَرِ الواحِدِ), and the indication of general wording (*dalalat al-ʿumum*, دَلالَةِ العُمُومِ). But this suspicion which must be acted upon has been strengthened by some means that makes acting upon it obligatory, so it rises above doubt and accusation.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is to suspect the people of goodness of evil. As for the people of evil and defiance, we may suspect them of the like of what has appeared from them.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: It is to suspect one's Muslim brother of evil, and there is no harm in it so long as one does not speak of it. If he speaks of that suspicion and reveals it, he sins.

Al-Qurtubi reported from most scholars that a bad suspicion of one whose outward state is good is not permissible, and that there is no blame in a bad suspicion of one whose outward state is bad. His saying, ﴿Indeed, some suspicion is sin﴾, is a justification for what precedes it, the command to avoid much suspicion. This "some" is the suspicion of evil about the people of goodness, and the sin is the punishment that the one who suspects deserves.

Among what indicates that this suspicion which is commanded to be avoided is restricted to suspicion of evil is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And you assumed an assumption of evil, and you were a people ruined﴾ [al-Fath: 12]. Therefore, nothing of the suspicion that is commanded to be followed in matters of religion enters into the suspicion commanded to be avoided, for God has made His servants worship by following it, and most scholars have held it obligatory to act upon it. None denied this except some sects of innovators, out of hostility to the religion and deviation from the majority of Muslims. The worship through suspicion has come in much of the purified Law, indeed in most of it.

Then, when God, glorified is He, commanded them to avoid much suspicion, He forbade them from spying, saying, ﴿And do not spy﴾. *Al-tajassus* (التَّجَسُّسُ) is searching for what is concealed from you of the faults and private matters of the Muslims. God, glorified is He, forbade them from searching for people's defects and shortcomings.

The majority read ﴿tajassasu﴾ with the *jim* (بِالجِيمِ), and its meaning is what we have mentioned. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Ibn Sirin read it with the *ha'* (بِالحاءِ).

Al-Akhfash said: Neither of them is far from the other, because *tajassus* with the *jim* is searching for what is concealed from you, and *tahassus* with the *ha'* is seeking news and searching for it.

It was also said: *tajassus* with the *jim* is searching, and from it comes the saying "a man is a *jasus*" (spy) when he searches out affairs. With the *ha'* it is what a person perceives through some of his senses.

It was said: with the *ha'* it is what a person seeks for himself, and with the *jim* it is to act as a messenger for another. This was said by Tha'lab.

﴿And let not some of you backbite others﴾. That is: let not some of you speak of others in their absence with what would displease them. *Al-ghibah* (الغِيبَةُ, backbiting) is that you mention a man with what he dislikes, as in the hadith of Abu Hurairah, established in the Sahih, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do you know what backbiting is?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "Your mentioning your brother with what he dislikes." It was said: "What if what I say is true of my brother?" He said: "If what you say is in him, then you have backbitten him, and if it is not in him, then you have slandered him."

﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾ He, glorified is He, likened backbiting to eating carrion, because the dead person does not know that his flesh is being eaten, just as the living person does not know of the backbiting done about him. Al-Zajjaj mentioned this meaning.

This passage contains an indication that a person's honour is like his flesh: just as eating his flesh is forbidden, so is overstepping against his honour. There is, in this, a warning against backbiting (al-ghība), a rebuke to the one who commits it, and a strong condemnation of him, which is clear. Human nature recoils from eating human flesh, and the human disposition finds it repugnant, quite apart from its being forbidden by the Law. Thus ﴿فَكَرِهْتُمُوهُ﴾ ("so you have disliked it"). Al-Farra' said: "Its implied reading is: ﴿فَقَدْ كَرِهْتُمُوهُ﴾ ('so you have indeed disliked it'), so do not do it." The meaning is: just as you dislike this, avoid mentioning your brother with evil in his absence. Al-Razi said: "The fa' (so) is in the sense of a response to a statement, as if he had said: 'None of you would love to eat the flesh of his brother; so you have disliked it, then.'"

Abu al-Baqa' said: "It is coordinated with an omitted element, its implied meaning being: 'This was presented to you, so you disliked it.'" ﴿وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ﴾ ("And fear Allah") by abandoning what He has commanded you to avoid. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ تَوَّابٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance, Merciful") toward whoever fears Him, for what has passed from him of sin and of opposing the command.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from Anas, who said: It was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If only you would visit Abdullah ibn Ubayy." So he set off to him, riding a donkey, and the Muslims set out walking, and the land was salty (sabakha). When he reached him, [Abdullah] said: "Keep away from me! By Allah, the smell of your donkey has harmed me." A man from the Ansar said: "By Allah, the donkey of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is better in smell than you!" Then men from his people became angry on behalf of Abdullah, and his companions became angry on behalf of each of them, so there was striking between them with palm-stalks, with hands and with sandals. Then there was revealed concerning them: ﴿وَإِن طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ ("And if two groups of the believers fight...") and so on.

Something similar has been related through other channels.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn Umar, who said: "I have not felt anything in myself as much as I felt about this verse: that I did not fight this rebellious group as Allah commanded me."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning the verse, who said: Allah commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers that when a group of believers fights, they should call them to the judgement of Allah and do justice between them. If they respond, he judges among them by the judgement of the Book of Allah until the wronged one is given justice. Whoever refuses to respond among them is a rebel (baghin), and it is incumbent upon the leader (imam) of the believers and the believers to fight them until they return to the command of Allah and acknowledge the judgement of Allah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿وَإِن طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ ("And if two groups of the believers fight..."), who said: There was fighting with sandals and staves, so He commanded them to reconcile between the two.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Aisha, who said: "I have not seen anything like what this nation has turned away from in this verse: ﴿وَإِن طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا فَأَصْلِحُوا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ ('And if two groups of the believers fight, then make reconciliation between them')."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muqatil concerning His saying: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا يَسْخَرْ قَوْمٌ مِّن قَوْمٍ﴾ ("O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people") that he said: It was revealed concerning a people from Banu Tamim who mocked Bilal, Salman, Ammar, Khabbab, Suhayb, Ibn Fuhayra and Salim, the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa.

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Dhamm al-Ghiba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَلْمِزُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ﴾ ("And do not defame one another") that he said: Let none of you slander another.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, the authors of the Four Sunan, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, transmitted from Abu Jabira ibn al-Dahhak, who said: "It was revealed concerning us, the Banu Salama: ﴿وَلَا تَنَابَزُوا بِالْأَلْقَابِ﴾ ('And do not insult one another by nicknames'). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came, and there was not a man among us except that he had two or three names. Whenever he called one of them by one of those names, they would say: 'O Messenger of Allah, he dislikes it!' So there was revealed: ﴿وَلَا تَنَابَزُوا بِالْأَلْقَابِ﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted something similar from Ibn Abbas.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: Mutual insulting by nicknames is that a man has committed evil deeds, then repented of them and returned to the truth, and Allah forbade that he be reproached for what had preceded from his deeds.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse, who said: If a man was a Jew and then embraced Islam, and [another] would say to him: "O Jew! O Christian! O Magian!", and would say to a Muslim man: "O sinner (fasiq)!"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اجْتَنِبُوا كَثِيرًا مِّنَ الظَّنِّ﴾ ("O you who have believed, avoid much of suspicion"), who said: Allah forbade the believer to suspect ill of a believer.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most false of speech. Do not spy, do not seek out secrets, do not compete one with another, do not envy one another, do not hate one another, and be servants of Allah as brothers. A man should not make an offer upon the offer of his brother until he marries or leaves [the matter]."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا﴾ ("And do not spy"), who said: Allah forbade the believer to pursue the faults (awrat) of a believer.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Zayd ibn Wahb, who said: Ibn Mas'ud was brought word, and it was said: "This is so-and-so, whose beard is dripping with wine!" Ibn Mas'ud said: "We have indeed been forbidden to spy, but if something becomes apparent to us, we will take it."

Traditions have also come down forbidding the pursuit of the faults of Muslims and spying upon their defects.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿وَلَا يَغْتَب بَّعْضُكُم بَعْضًا﴾ ("And let not some of you backbite others") to the end of the verse, who said: Allah has forbidden that a believer be backbitten about anything, just as He forbade carrion.

The traditions on the prohibition of backbiting are very numerous and well known in the books of hadith.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 49, verses 9–12 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read *iqtatalu* (اقْتَتَلُوا) with the plural, taking into account each individual member of the two groups, as in His saying, ﴿These are two adversaries who dispute﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. The pronoun in His saying *baynahuma* (بَيْنَهُما, "between them") refers to the two groups, taking into account the wording.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read *iqtatalata* (اقْتَتَلَتا), taking into account the wording *taifatan* (طائِفَتانِ, "two groups"). Zayd ibn ʿAli and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read *iqtatala* (اقْتَتَلا), and the masculine verb in this reading is taking into account "the two parties" (al-fariqayn) or "the two companies" (al-rahtayn).

*Al-baghy* (البَغْيُ, transgression) is aggression without right, and refusing reconciliation that is in accordance with what is correct. *Al-fayʾ* (الفَيْءُ) is returning. The meaning is: if two groups of Muslims fight, the Muslims must strive for reconciliation between them and call them to the judgment of God. If, after that, one of the two groups commits aggression against the other and does not accept reconciliation nor enter into it, then the Muslims must fight this transgressing group until it returns to the command and judgment of God. If that transgressing group returns from its transgression and responds to the call to the Book of God and His judgment, then the Muslims must act justly between the two groups in judgment, seek out what is correct and in accordance with the judgment of God, and restrain the hand of the wrongdoing group until it leaves injustice and discharges what it owes to the other.

Then God, glorified is He, commanded the Muslims to act justly in all their affairs, after commanding them with this particular justice concerning the two fighting groups. He said, ﴿And act justly; indeed, God loves those who act justly﴾. That is: and be just, for God loves the just, and His love for them entails rewarding them with the best reward.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: ﴿So make reconciliation between them﴾ by calling them to the judgment of the Book of God and agreeing to what is in it, for them and against them. ﴿And if one of them transgresses against the other﴾ and seeks what is not its right and does not return to reconciliation, ﴿then fight the one that transgresses﴾ until it returns to the obedience of God and to the reconciliation that God has commanded.

The sentence ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ is a resumptive clause, confirming what precedes it of the command to reconciliation. The meaning is that they all go back to one origin, which is faith.

Al-Zajjaj said: Religion unites them, so they are brothers when they agree in their religion. They return by agreement in religion to the origin of lineage, since they all descend from Adam and Eve. ﴿So make reconciliation between your two brothers﴾ means every two Muslims who dispute and fight. The specification of two in mention is to establish the obligation of reconciliation for more than two by way of greater priority.

The majority read *bayna akhawaykum* (بَيْنَ أخَوَيْكم) in the dual. Zayd ibn Thabit, ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, al-Hasan, Hammad ibn Salamah and Ibn Sirin read *ikhwanikum* (إخْوانِكم) in the plural. It is reported from Abu ʿUmar, Nasr ibn ʿAsim, Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Jahdari and Yaʿqub that they read *bayna ikhwatikum* (بَيْنَ إخْوَتِكم) with the feminine-plural form, also in the plural.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi, in explaining the majority reading, said: He meant by the "two brothers" the two groups, because the dual form may be used and intend plurality.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: That is, make reconciliation between every two brothers. ﴿And fear God﴾ in all your affairs, ﴿that you may be shown mercy﴾ through piety. The expression of hope (*tarajji*, التَّرَجِّي) is with respect to those addressed, that is, hoping that you will be shown mercy.

In this verse is evidence for fighting the transgressing faction when its transgression is established against the imam or against any one of the Muslims. It also refutes the view of one who holds that fighting is not permissible, citing His saying (ﷺ): "Fighting a Muslim is disbelief." The intended meaning of this hadith and what has come in its sense is fighting a Muslim who does not transgress.

Ibn Jarir said: If the obligation, in every dispute that occurs between two groups of Muslims, were to flee from it and to remain in one's dwellings, then no right would be established and no falsehood would be annulled. The people of hypocrisy and immorality would find a means to make lawful everything that God has forbidden them: the wealth of the Muslims, the taking of their women captive, and the shedding of their blood, by forming factions against them, while the Muslims restrain their hands from them. This contradicts His saying (ﷺ): "Take hold of the hands of your foolish ones."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This verse is a foundation for fighting among Muslims and a principal reference in fighting those who interpret (the texts) in error. The Companions relied upon it, the notables of the religious community resorted to it, and it is what the Prophet (ﷺ) meant by his saying: "The transgressing faction will kill ʿAmmar." It is also what he (ﷺ) meant concerning the Kharijites: "They will come out at a time of division among the people, and the party nearer to the truth will kill them."

﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule another people, perhaps they are better than them﴾. *Al-sukhriyyah* (السُّخْرِيَةُ) is mockery, *al-istihza'* (الِاسْتِهْزاءُ). Abu Zayd reported: *sakhirtu bihi*, *dahiktu bihi* and *hazi'tu bihi* (I mocked him, I laughed at him, and I scoffed at him).

Al-Akhfash said: *sakhirtu minhu* and *sakhirtu bihi*, *dahiktu minhu* and *dahiktu bihi*, *hazi'tu minhu* and *hazi'tu bihi* are all said. The noun is *al-sukhriyyah* and *al-sukhra*, and both were read in His saying, ﴿that some of them may take others in service [sukhriyyan]﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32].

The meaning of the verse is a prohibition to the believers from one of them mocking another. He gave the reason for this prohibition with His saying, ﴿perhaps they are better than them﴾, that is, that the one being mocked may be better in the sight of God than those who mock him.

Since the word *qawm* (قَوْمٌ, "people") is specific to men, because they are the ones who take charge over women, He mentioned women separately, saying, ﴿nor women [of] women﴾, that is, let not women mock women, ﴿perhaps they are better than them﴾, meaning better than the women who mock them. It was said that He mentioned women separately because mockery among them is more frequent.

﴿And do not defame one another﴾. *Al-lamz* (اللَّمْزُ) is faultfinding. Its verification has already passed in Surah Bara'ah, at His saying, ﴿And among them are those who criticize you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58].

Ibn Jarir said: *Al-lamz* is by hand, eye, tongue and gesture, while *al-hamz* (الهَمْزُ) is only by tongue. Mujahid, Qatadah and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: Let none of you slander another.

Al-Dahhak said: Let none of you curse another.
